title: 〜そして (at the start: and then / and also)
meaning: Links two sentences or two items. It shows the order of actions, or adds one more point to what came before.
connection: Sentence. そして、sentence / Noun、そして noun

senses.label: Sequence: and then
senses.meaning: Actions happen one after another in time, like “and then” or “next”. Usually the same person does both actions. It sounds a little more formal than 「それから」.
senses.connection: Action sentence. そして、action sentence (often with 「まず」 and 「最後に」)
examples: I ate breakfast. And then I went to school.
First, wash your hands. Then cook the food.

senses.label: Adding: and also
senses.meaning: Adds one more item to what you just said, like “and also” or “what's more”. Often used to list features of a person or thing.
senses.connection: Adjective / noun sentence. そして、adjective / noun sentence
examples: This room is spacious. And it's very bright, too.
I can speak Japanese, English, and Chinese.

senses.label: Result: and so
senses.meaning: Something develops from what came before and leads to a result, like “and so” or “in the end”. Common in stories and written texts.
senses.connection: Narrative sentence. そして、result sentence (usually in the た-form)
examples: He practiced every day. And he won the match.
The two of them met. And then they got married.

notes: A comma 「、」 usually follows 「そして」, though people often skip it in speech.
「そして」 only links ideas that go in the same direction. It can't mean “but”. For contrast, use 「でも」 or 「しかし」.
To link two actions in order, you can also use the te-form: 「朝ご飯を食べて、学校へ行きました」. It sounds tighter.

daily.title: Talking about your day
daily.description: Telling a friend, or writing in a diary, what you did in order.
daily.example: Yesterday I went shopping. And then I saw a movie.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: Adding more information about yourself.
daily.example: I'm a student. I also work part-time at a café.

daily.title: Reading a fairy tale
daily.description: Fairy tales and picture books often use 「そして」 to move the story forward.
daily.example: And they lived happily ever after.

work.title: Explaining steps
work.description: Walking a coworker or client through how to do something.
work.example: Press this button. Then please enter your name.

work.title: Wrapping up a talk
work.description: Listing key points in a speech and adding one last item.
work.example: Quality, price, and service are all important.

etymology: Generally thought to be a shortened form of 「そうして」: the adverb 「そう」 (that way) plus 「して」, the te-form of 「する」. It first meant “having done so”, and later became fixed as a conjunction.

similar.title: 〜それから
similar.explanation: Both can mean “and then”. 「それから」 puts more weight on “after that” in time, and is also used to add a new topic (“also”). 「そして」 fits more naturally for adding points or showing a result, and sounds a bit more written.

similar.title: 〜て (sequence)
similar.explanation: The te-form links actions inside one sentence. 「そして」 comes at the start of a sentence and joins two separate sentences.

similar.title: 〜しかし
similar.explanation: 「しかし」 means “however”: the second sentence goes against the first. 「そして」 continues or adds in the same direction.

title: 〜それから (at the start: after that / also)
meaning: Shows time order (“after that”). It is also used to add something (“also”, “and”).
connection: Sentence. それから、sentence / Noun、それから noun

senses.label: Time: after that
senses.meaning: You do one thing after finishing another, like “then” or “after that”. The focus is on the order in time.
senses.connection: Action sentence. それから、action sentence
examples: I got up at seven. Then I took a shower.
I walk to the station, and then take a bus.

senses.label: Adding: also
senses.meaning: Adds another item to what you've already said, like “also” or “and”. Common when ordering food or listing things.
senses.connection: Noun / sentence. それから、what you add
examples: Two coffees, and one piece of cake, please.
Also, please come at eight tomorrow.

senses.label: Ever since then
senses.meaning: A state that has continued from a certain point in time, like “since then”. Usually followed by something ongoing.
senses.connection: Talking about the past. それから(は)、ongoing state
examples: I came to Japan last year. Since then, I've been living in Tokyo.

notes: 「それから」 can also stand alone as a question: 「それから？」 (And then?). It urges the other person to keep talking.
Literally, 「それから」 means “from that”. In 「それから選んでください」 (Please choose from those), it is used literally, not as a conjunction.

daily.title: Ordering food
daily.description: Ordering dishes one by one at a restaurant.
daily.example: One ramen. And a beer too, please.

daily.title: Listening to a friend's story
daily.description: Urging a friend to go on with a story.
daily.example: Uh-huh, and then?

daily.title: Weekend plans
daily.description: Telling your family what you'll do, in order.
daily.example: On Saturday I'm going to the library. After that, I'm meeting a friend.

work.title: Adding an item at a meeting
work.description: Adding one more announcement before a meeting ends.
work.example: Also, next week's meeting will be on the third floor.

work.title: Explaining the order of tasks
work.description: A senior coworker explains the order of work to a newcomer.
work.example: First check your email, and then please make the documents.

etymology: Made from the pronoun 「それ」 (that) and the particle 「から」 (from), literally “from that (point in time)”. It grew into a conjunction meaning “after that” and “also”.

similar.title: 〜そして
similar.explanation: 「そして」 focuses on continuing, adding, or a result. 「それから」 focuses on “after that” in time and on adding topics; it is more common in speech.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「〜てから」 stresses “do A first, then B” within one sentence. 「それから」 starts a new sentence and links two sentences.

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: 「から」 after a noun marks a starting point. 「それから」 has become a single conjunction meaning “then” or “also”.

title: 〜と (quotation: 〜と言う・〜と思う)
meaning: The quoting particle 「と」. It comes after what someone says or thinks, followed by a verb like 「言う」, 「思う」, or 「聞く」.
connection: 「Direct quote」 / plain-form sentence + と + 言う・思う・聞く・書く etc.

senses.label: Direct quotation
senses.meaning: Quotes someone's exact words, placed inside 「」, like “say, ‘...’”. Keep the original style (です・ます etc.) as it was.
senses.connection: 「Exact words」 + と + 言う／言いました
examples: The teacher said, “There's a test tomorrow.”
I said “thank you” to my friend.

senses.label: Indirect quotation
senses.meaning: Reports what someone said in your own words, using the plain form, like “say that ...”. Add 「だ」 after nouns and na-adjectives.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence (noun / na-adjective + だ) + と + 言う／言っていた
examples: Mr. Tanaka said he isn't coming tomorrow.
My mother says she likes this shop.

senses.label: Thoughts and opinions
senses.meaning: 「と思う」 gives the speaker's thought or judgment, like “I think”. It sounds softer than stating something flatly.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence (noun / na-adjective + だ) + と + 思う／思います
examples: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think this movie is interesting.
I think he's a student.

senses.label: Hearing, writing, and more
senses.meaning: 「と」 also goes with 「聞く」, 「書く」, 「答える」, 「呼ぶ」 and similar verbs, to give what was heard, written, answered, or what something is called.
senses.connection: Content + と + 聞く・書く・答える・呼ぶ・伝える
examples: I heard on the news that a typhoon is coming.
I wrote “thank you” in the letter.
He answered, “Yes.”

notes: In indirect quotes, add 「だ」 after nouns and na-adjectives: 「学生だと思う」, not ✕「学生と思う」.
「と思う」 is for the speaker's own thoughts. For a third person's thoughts, use 「と思っている」.
The 「と」 meaning “and / with” (友達と話す) is not a quote. Check whether a verb like 「言う」 or 「思う」 follows.
In casual speech, the quoting 「と」 often becomes 「って」: 「行くって言った」.

daily.title: Passing on a family member's words
daily.description: Telling a friend what someone in your family said.
daily.example: My older sister said she was going to bed.

daily.title: Sharing your impressions
daily.description: Giving your opinion after a movie.
daily.example: I think the last scene was good.

daily.title: Asking how to say something
daily.description: Asking what something is called in Japanese.
daily.example: What do you call this in Japanese?

work.title: Giving your opinion at a meeting
work.description: Using 「と思います」 to state your view politely.
work.example: I think this plan is good.

work.title: Passing on a phone message
work.description: Telling your boss what a client said on the phone.
work.example: Mr. Yamada called to say he'll be a little late for the meeting.

etymology: The quoting 「と」 has the same origin as the 「と」 meaning “and / with”. Since ancient times it has introduced what is said or thought (as in classical 「〜と言ふ」 and 「〜と思ふ」). It is one of the oldest uses in Japanese.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: 「〜と言う」 is the most typical pairing and focuses on quoting speech. This entry looks at the particle 「と」 itself and the many verbs it can go with.

similar.title: 〜と思う
similar.explanation: 「〜と思う」 is only for the speaker's thoughts. The quoting 「と」 also works with 「言う」, 「聞く」, 「書く」 and more.

similar.title: 〜と (and / with)
similar.explanation: In 「友達と行く」, 「と」 means “with”, and a person or thing comes before it. The quoting 「と」 comes after a sentence or a stretch of speech.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation / topic)
similar.explanation: 「って」 is the casual form of 「と」, common among friends. Use 「と」 in formal situations.

title: 〜 verb + noun (verbs describing nouns: relative clauses)
meaning: Put a verb's plain form right before a noun to describe it. It works like an English relative clause (“the book that I bought”), but the clause comes before the noun.
connection: Verb plain form (dictionary form / た-form / ている-form / ない-form) + noun

senses.label: Dictionary form
senses.meaning: Describes a habit, something planned, or a general fact, like “the ... that (will) do”. The verb links straight to the noun with no 「の」 in between.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + noun (人・所・時・日 etc.)
examples: I bought the milk I drink every morning.
Who is the person going to Japan?

senses.label: た-form
senses.meaning: Describes something that happened in the past, or a state left after an action, like “the ... that did”.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + noun
examples: This is the book I bought yesterday.
The person wearing glasses is the teacher.

senses.label: ている-form
senses.meaning: Describes an action in progress or an ongoing state, like “the ... that is doing”.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + noun
examples: The person reading a newspaper over there is Mr. Tanaka.
The town I live in is quiet.

senses.label: ない-form
senses.meaning: Describes something negative, like “the ... that doesn't”.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + noun
examples: I look up words I don't know in the dictionary.
Please call the people who didn't come.

notes: English says “the book I bought”, with the noun first. Japanese puts the clause first: 「私が買った本」. Don't put 「の」 between the verb and the noun: ✕「買ったの本」.
Inside the describing clause, mark the subject with 「が」 (or 「の」), not 「は」: 「私が作った料理」.
Use the plain form before a noun, not the ます-form: ✕「昨日買いました本」.

daily.title: Looking for someone
daily.description: Describing a person to a friend in a crowd.
daily.example: The person wearing red clothes over there is my younger sister.

daily.title: Showing something
daily.description: Showing a friend a souvenir you bought on a trip.
daily.example: This is a souvenir I bought in Kyoto.

daily.title: Finding a place
daily.description: Talking with a friend about where to eat.
daily.example: Do you know a place where you can eat cheap, tasty food?

work.title: Checking meeting materials
work.description: Asking a coworker where the materials for a meeting are.
work.example: Where are the materials for tomorrow's meeting?

work.title: Introducing the person in charge
work.description: Introducing yourself to a client as the person handling a project.
work.example: I'm Sato, in charge of this project.

etymology: In classical Japanese, verbs had two separate forms: the conclusive form (shūshikei) to end a sentence, and the attributive form (rentaikei) to describe nouns. In modern Japanese the two merged, so the plain form can now describe a noun directly.

similar.title: 〜 (verb plain form) + noun (relative clause)
similar.explanation: Both entries cover the same structure. This one sorts the meanings by verb form (dictionary, た, ている, ない).

similar.title: 〜な + noun
similar.explanation: A na-adjective needs 「な」 before a noun (静かな町). A verb links to a noun directly, with nothing in between.

similar.title: 〜の (possession / describing)
similar.explanation: A noun describes another noun with 「の」 (日本の車). A verb describing a noun takes no 「の」. Adding one is a very common learner mistake.

similar.title: 〜の (replacing が)
similar.explanation: Inside a describing clause, the subject 「が」 can become 「の」: 「私が買った本」＝「私の買った本」.

title: 〜の (replacing が in a relative clause)
meaning: In a clause that describes a noun, the subject marker 「が」 can be replaced with 「の」. The meaning stays the same.
connection: Noun + の + plain-form verb / adjective + noun

senses.label: Verb clauses
senses.meaning: 「の」 marks the subject (the doer) of the clause. 「母の作った料理」＝「母が作った料理」. It sounds a little more literary and gentle.
senses.connection: Noun + の + verb plain form + noun
examples: The food my mother makes is delicious.
This is the town where I was born.
On rainy days, I stay home.

senses.label: Adjective clauses
senses.meaning: When describing a person or thing, 「〜が + adjective + noun」 is often said as 「〜の + adjective + noun」. Many of these are set expressions.
senses.connection: Noun + の + i-adjective / na-adjective + noun
examples: The tall person is my older brother.
Did you see a girl with long hair?

notes: You can only swap 「が」 for 「の」 inside a clause that describes a noun. The subject of the main sentence can't change: ✕「母の料理を作った」 means something completely different.
If an object with 「を」 comes between 「が」 and the noun, 「の」 is usually not used: say 「母が子どもにご飯を作った日」, not 「母の」.
In 「私の作った」, 「の」 does not mean “my”. It marks the subject: “that I made”. Be careful when translating.

daily.title: Talking about your hometown
daily.description: Telling a friend about the place where you grew up.
daily.example: This is the town where I grew up.

daily.title: Describing someone's looks
daily.description: Describing what a person looks like to a friend.
daily.example: The girl with big eyes is my younger sister.

daily.title: Reading novels
daily.description: Novels and song lyrics often use the literary 「〜の + verb + noun」.
daily.example: I want to go to the town where you live.

work.title: Citing a document
work.example: This is the report the department manager wrote.

work.title: Presenting products
work.description: Presenting products customers chose at a product briefing.
work.example: Let me introduce the products our customers chose.

etymology: In classical Japanese, both 「の」 and 「が」 could mark the subject, and both could show possession. In modern Japanese, 「が」 mainly marks the subject, but the old subject use of 「の」 survives in clauses that describe nouns.

similar.title: 〜が (subject)
similar.explanation: 「が」 can mark the subject in any sentence. 「の」 can replace 「が」 only in a clause that describes a noun.

similar.title: 〜の (possession / describing)
similar.explanation: In 「私の本」, 「の」 shows possession (my book). In 「私の買った本」, 「の」 marks the subject (the book I bought). Check whether a verb or adjective follows 「の」.

similar.title: 〜 verb + noun
similar.explanation: Verbs describing nouns is the overall structure. This entry covers just one point: the subject can be marked with 「の」.

title: 〜の前・〜の上・〜の中 (position words)
meaning: Use “noun + の + position word” to say where something is: on the desk, in front of the station, inside the box.
connection: Noun + の + 前・上・中・下・横・隣 etc. + に／で／を

senses.label: Above, below, inside, outside
senses.meaning: Gives a position relative to something: on, under, inside, outside. 「の」 is required: 「机の上」 (on the desk), literally “the desk's top”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 上・下・中・外 + に (existence) ／ で (action)
examples: There's a book on the desk.
My wallet is in the bag.
There's a cat under the bed.

senses.label: Front, back, left, right
senses.meaning: Gives directions such as in front, behind, left, right, and beside. 「横」 is simply “beside”; 「隣」 means “next door” or right next to something of the same kind.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 前・後ろ・右・左・横・隣・そば
examples: I'm waiting in front of the station.
There's a convenience store next to the bank.
Please stand behind Mr. Tanaka.

senses.label: Between and near
senses.meaning: 「間」 means “between two things”, usually as 「AとBの間」. 「近く」 and 「そば」 mean “near”.
senses.connection: AとB + の + 間 ／ Noun + の + 近く・そば
examples: There's a park between the post office and the hospital.
There's a supermarket near my house.

notes: For existence, use 「〜の上に〜がある／いる」. For the place of an action, use 「〜の前で〜する」.
「の前」 can also mean “before” in time: 「食事の前に手を洗う」. Use the context to tell place from time.
「〜の中で一番〜」 is a comparison pattern meaning “the most ... among”. It doesn't mean “inside” a place.
Position words can also be used alone as nouns: 「上を見てください」.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: A family member asks where the keys are.
daily.example: The keys are on the table.

daily.title: Choosing a meeting place
daily.description: Deciding with a friend where to meet.
daily.example: OK, let's meet in front of the station.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: Telling someone on the street where a place is.
daily.example: The library is on the other side of the park.

work.title: Explaining where a room is
work.description: Telling a visitor where the meeting room is.
work.example: The meeting room is to the right of the elevator.

work.title: Finding documents
work.description: Telling a coworker where you put some documents.
work.example: The documents are in the drawer of my desk.

etymology: Position words like 「前」, 「上」, and 「中」 are nouns themselves. So, like any noun, they are described with “noun + の”. Literally, it's “the desk's top” or “the station's front”.

similar.title: 〜の (possession / describing)
similar.explanation: The 「の」 here is the same 「の」 that links two nouns. The second noun just happens to be a position word.

similar.title: 〜は〜にある・いる
similar.explanation: 「〜は〜の上にある」 combines both: this entry gives the exact position, and 「にある・いる」 says that something exists there.

similar.title: 〜の中で〜がいちばん
similar.explanation: 「〜の中で一番」 means “the most ... within a group” and is a comparison. In this entry, 「の中」 means physically “inside”.

title: 〜 dropping particles (casual speech)
meaning: In everyday conversation, particles like 「は」, 「を」, 「が」, and 「へ・に」 are often dropped. This makes speech sound casual and friendly.
connection: Noun (は・を・が・へ dropped) + predicate (mostly casual, plain form)

senses.label: Dropping 「は」
senses.meaning: The 「は」 after a topic is often dropped and replaced by a pause or comma. Common when introducing yourself or pointing at something. It sounds relaxed and natural.
senses.connection: 私・これ・それ etc. + (は)、 + predicate
examples: I'm Tanaka.
This is good, isn't it?

senses.label: Dropping 「を」
senses.meaning: The 「を」 after an object is very often dropped in speech, especially in everyday questions like 「ご飯食べた？」.
senses.connection: Noun + (を) + 食べる・飲む・見る・する etc.
examples: Have you eaten?
Want some tea?
Did you do your homework?

senses.label: Dropping 「が」
senses.meaning: The 「が」 for existence, states, and natural events is also often dropped, as in “I'm hungry” or “I have no time”.
senses.connection: Noun + (が) + ある・ない・すく・降る etc.
examples: I'm hungry.
I don't have time today.

senses.label: Dropping 「へ・に」
senses.meaning: The 「へ」 or 「に」 for a destination is also often dropped in speech before 「行く」, 「来る」, or 「帰る」.
senses.connection: Place noun + (へ・に) + 行く・来る・帰る
examples: Are you going to school tomorrow?
Where are you going?

notes: Only drop particles in casual talk with friends and family. Don't drop them in formal situations, in writing, or when speaking to superiors.
Particles with specific meanings, like 「で」, 「から」, 「まで」, and 「と」, usually can't be dropped, or the meaning becomes unclear.
Without particles, the meaning depends mostly on context. Beginners should first master the full forms with particles.

daily.title: Questions at home
daily.description: A mother asks her child whether they've eaten.
daily.example: Have you eaten?

daily.title: Inviting a friend out
daily.description: Casually asking a friend if they want to go somewhere.
daily.example: Want to go see a movie this weekend?

daily.title: Watching Japanese dramas and anime
daily.description: Dialogue on screen often drops particles, so fill in the meaning as you listen.
daily.example: Man, I'm starving.

work.title: Chatting with a close coworker
work.description: Talking casually with a coworker you know well at lunch.

etymology: In Japanese, word order and context are often enough to show how the parts of a sentence relate. So in speech, obvious particles tend to be dropped. This is generally seen as a natural feature of speech aiming for brevity and closeness, not a grammar mistake.

similar.title: 〜は (topic)
similar.explanation: In writing and polite speech, 「は」 should be used. In casual speech it is often dropped and replaced by a pause.

similar.title: 〜を (object)
similar.explanation: 「を」 is the particle most easily dropped in speech, but it must be written in formal texts.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation / topic)
similar.explanation: In speech, 「って」 often replaces 「は」 to raise a topic (「田中さんって、どんな人？」). This isn't dropping a particle; it's switching to a casual one.
